questions.prompt: What should the body property of a SwiftUI view ideally be?

options.text: A fast, lightweight, and pure description of the user interface.
options.explanation: View bodies run frequently on the main thread and must execute rapidly.

options.text: An asynchronous worker performing network and file operations.
options.explanation: Body is a synchronous property and must never block for network or file I/O.

options.text: A cache holding reference type database connections.
options.explanation: Database connections belong in data layer services, not view bodies.

options.text: A persistent controller managing the UIKit window hierarchy.
options.explanation: SwiftUI views are ephemeral value types, not persistent window managers.

questions.prompt: Why is performing heavy array sorting inside a view body considered an anti-pattern?

options.text: Because Swift arrays cannot be sorted within view struct declarations.
options.explanation: Arrays can be sorted syntactically, but doing so wastes main thread time.

options.text: Because body runs repeatedly, blocking the main thread and dropping frames.
options.explanation: Sorting on every render pass consumes CPU cycles and causes stutter.

options.text: Because sorting an array permanently deletes its underlying elements.
options.explanation: Sorting transforms element ordering without deleting items.

options.text: Because SwiftUI views automatically convert all arrays into hash sets.
options.explanation: SwiftUI does not convert arrays into hash sets.

questions.prompt: Where should expensive operations like sorting, filtering, and date formatting be performed?

options.text: Inside custom property wrappers attached to primitive view bodies.
options.explanation: Property wrappers decorate state but should not perform heavy sorting in body.

options.text: Within the body getter of the immediate parent navigation stack.
options.explanation: Parent view bodies also run on the main thread and must stay lightweight.

options.text: In view models, background tasks, or cached properties beforehand.
options.explanation: Pre-computing derived data keeps the view body fast and responsive.

options.text: Directly inside view initializer parameters on every single redraw.
options.explanation: Initializers are called frequently during parent body evaluations.

questions.prompt: What does SwiftUI do in the render loop after executing invalidated view bodies?

options.text: It completely reloads the entire root application view controller.
options.explanation: SwiftUI performs targeted local updates rather than reloading the app.

options.text: It wipes all user interaction states and resets text fields.
options.explanation: Preserving view identity protects interaction state and text input.

options.text: It converts all subviews into static PNG bitmaps on disk.
options.explanation: SwiftUI renders dynamic vector views to display buffers, not PNG files.

options.text: It diffs new view structs against old ones and renders visual changes.
options.explanation: Diffing identifies the minimal necessary updates to commit to the screen.

questions.prompt: How does conforming a subview to Equatable and applying .equatable() optimize performance?

options.text: SwiftUI can compare inputs and skip body evaluation if properties match.
options.explanation: Equatable comparison prevents redundant body evaluations when inputs are equal.

options.text: It forces SwiftUI to execute the subview body on a background thread.
options.explanation: View bodies always execute on the main thread, never in the background.

options.text: It caches the view in disk storage across distinct application launches.
options.explanation: Equatable affects memory diffing during runtime, not disk persistence.

options.text: It prevents the child view from ever receiving state updates again.
options.explanation: The view still updates whenever any of its properties actually change.

questions.prompt: How does modern @Observable improve upon older ObservableObject performance?

options.text: By compressing memory payloads through background zip operations.
options.explanation: Observation does not compress memory using zip operations.

options.text: By tracking property reads per view rather than invalidating for any change.
options.explanation: @Observable scopes invalidations strictly to views that read the modified property.

options.text: By executing view body calculations directly on the GPU hardware.
options.explanation: View bodies evaluate on the CPU before GPU render passes occur.

options.text: By converting all model classes into immutable value structs at runtime.
options.explanation: @Observable works on reference classes without turning them into structs.

options.text: The app runs out of UUID numbers and throws a memory allocation fault.
options.explanation: UUID space is vast and does not run out, but randomness destroys identity.

options.text: The compiler refuses to build views that instantiate UUID objects.
options.explanation: The code compiles cleanly, but runtime performance degrades severely.

options.text: Every render generates new IDs, destroying view state and forcing rebuilds.
options.explanation: Unstable identity causes SwiftUI to tear down and reconstruct all subviews.

options.text: SwiftUI converts the list into an unscrollable static image container.
options.explanation: The list remains scrollable, but drops frames due to view churn.

questions.prompt: How does fine-grained observation in iOS 17+ reduce unnecessary body invalidations?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

options.text: By offloading all SwiftUI view struct evaluations to background dispatch queues.
options.explanation: View bodies remain on the main actor; observation optimizes dependency scoping.

options.text: By rasterizing non-visible views to vector PDF format behind the scenes.
options.explanation: Observation tracks runtime property reads, not vector rendering.

options.text: By disabling view animations whenever model properties change values.

options.text: By establishing dependencies only for properties actually read during body execution.
options.explanation: Unread properties never trigger invalidation, eliminating broadcast updates.

questions.prompt: Explain why keeping view body execution fast and lightweight is critical in SwiftUI apps. Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that view body executes synchronously on the main thread during render passes
Explains that heavy computations in body cause main thread blocking and dropped frames

questions.modelAnswer: SwiftUI evaluates view bodies synchronously on the main thread whenever dependent state changes. If a view body performs heavy computations like sorting, filtering, or JSON parsing, it stalls the main thread. This delay causes dropped frames and stuttering during scrolling and animations. Keeping view bodies fast makes sure the app maintains a smooth 60 or 120 frames per second.

questions.prompt: How does conforming subviews to Equatable and using .equatable() help avoid unnecessary body evaluations? Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Equatable allows SwiftUI to compare view property values between render passes
Explains that matching properties allow SwiftUI to skip executing the subview body

questions.modelAnswer: By conforming a subview to Equatable and applying the .equatable() modifier, you allow SwiftUI to compare old and new view struct inputs. If parent state changes but the subview properties remain identical, SwiftUI skips executing the child view body completely. This optimization prevents wasted work across complex view hierarchies when parent state changes frequently.

questions.prompt: Describe why generating UUID() inside ForEach identity causes performance problems in SwiftUI lists. Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that generating UUID() inside body creates random IDs on every evaluation pass
Explains that unstable identity destroys view state and forces complete reconstruction of subviews

questions.modelAnswer: Generating UUID() inside a view body creates new random identifiers on every single evaluation pass. Because the identifiers change constantly, SwiftUI cannot match old views to new views in its render graph. This unstable identity causes SwiftUI to tear down existing views, destroy internal state, and reconstruct the entire list from scratch. Always use stable, persistent identifiers from your data models.

questions.prompt: How does the Observation framework in iOS 17+ improve performance compared to Combine-based ObservableObject? Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

rubric.criterion: Explains that ObservableObject invalidates any observing view whenever any Published property changes
Explains that @Observable tracks per-property access so only views reading the changed property re-evaluate

questions.modelAnswer: With older ObservableObject and @Published, changing any property triggers objectWillChange, invalidating every view that observes the object regardless of which property it displays. In contrast, the modern @Observable macro uses the Observation framework to track property access on a granular per-property basis. Views only re-evaluate when the specific properties they access in body change. This fine-grained scoping eliminates wasted body evaluations across the application.

questions.prompt: Explain the role of Self._printChanges() when diagnosing SwiftUI performance hitches. Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that calling Self._printChanges() inside body logs which dependency caused the view update
Explains that it helps developers detect unexpected state changes and over-invalidation loops

questions.modelAnswer: Calling Self._printChanges() inside a view body logs the exact state property, binding, or environment key that caused SwiftUI to re-evaluate the view. It helps developers discover unnecessary updates and over-invalidation cycles during debugging. By knowing which dependency changed, engineers can quickly scope or isolate states that cause dropped frames.
